Writ Petition No. 57 of 1989
Writ Petition No. 1897 of 1991
lawyer:
Nazmul Huda with Sigma Huda and SAM Mahbub Elahi, Advocates — For the Petitioners. 
No one — For the Respondents.
parties:
General Manager, Sirajganj Biddyut Samity and others ------ Petitioners
Vs.
Chairman, Labour Court, Rajshahi and ors ------ Respondents
full_judgment:
MA Aziz J: This Rule was issued calling upon the respondents to show cause why the impugned ex-parte judgment and order dated 2-2-89 (Annexure-B) passed in complaint Case No. 53 of 1988 by respondent No. 1 (Chairman Labour Court, Rajshahi) should not be declared to have been made without lawful authority and to be of no legal effect. 

 (c) that the Samity drew up departmental proceeding against respondent No. 2 on charge of insubordination, inefficiency, theft, misuse of powers and misconduct under section 17 of the Standing Orders Act. Thereafter he was placed under suspension under section 18 of the aforesaid Act and eventually after a full-dress enquiry respondent No. 2 was found guilty and on the basis of the recommendation of the Enquiry Committee he was dismissed from service by petitioner No. 1 (General Manager, Palli Biddyut Samity) by order dated 15-11-88. 

 (d) that against the order of dismissal as aforesaid respondent No. 2 as first party filed a complaint case in the court of respondent No. 1 under section 25(a) of the Standing Orders Act challenging the legality of the order of dismissal. The said petition of complaint was registered as Complaint Case No. 53 of 1988 (Annexure-A). 

 (e) that 15-1-89 was fixed for filing written statement by the second party but they having been found absent, 2-2-89 was fixed for ex-parte disposal of the case. 

 3. On the appointed date i.e. 2-2-89, the case was taken up for hearing. Respondent No. 2 as first party was examined as the lone witness and papers submitted by him were marked as Ext. 1-7. The Labour Court by order dated 2-2-89 set aside the order of dismissal dated 15-11-88 directing the second party petitioners to reinstate him in service within 30 days with all back wages. 

 4. It is contended by the petitioners that they had no knowledge about complaint case No. 53 of 1988 and, as such, they were not aware of the ex-parte order dated 2-2-89 that they came to know about the ex-parte order after a long time when the learned Advocate for the first party (respondent No. 2 Md Mokaddas Ali Miah) sent to them a certified copy of the order dated 2-2-89 with a forwarding. 

 5. Thereafter the petitioners (second party) filed as application on 4-2-89 under Order 9 rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure to have complaint case No. 53 of 1988 restored to its file and number which was registered as Miscellaneous Case No. 2 of 1989 but the same was dismissed by order dated 21-6-89. 

 6. The second party instead of challenging the order of dismissal dated 21-6-89 of Miscellaneous Case No. 2 of 1989 have filed the present writ petition challenging the legality of the ex-parte order dated 2-2-89 passed in complaint case No. 53 of 1988. 

 7. Mr Nazmul Huda, learned Counsel appearing along with learned Advocates Mrs Sigma Huda and Mr SAM Mahbub Elahi for the second party petitioners, submits that respondent No. 1 (Chairman, Labour Court) erred in law and on facts in disposing of the complaint case ex-parte without giving any finding as to whether notices upon the second parties were duly served and received. He further submits that the order sheet on this vital point is totally silent. Mr Huda next submits that the order of dismissal dated 15-11-88 on the basis of recommendation of petitioner No. 2 i.e. the Assistant General Manager (General Services) Sirajganj Palli Bidyut Samity on the ground of misconduct should not have been so lightly interfered with without making further inquiry as to whether service return was received or not. 

 8. The learned Counsel also argued that Annexure-B (the ex-parte order) passed by the Labour Court has adversely affected the internal administration of the Bidyut Samity. He further submits that law and equity demand that the impugned order should be struck down and the case be heard de-novo by affording an opportunity to the petitioner to place their case before the Labour Court. 

 10. The second party in the complaint case namely, the writ petitioners, in their prayer portion made the following prayers: 

 "A) Issue a Rule Nisi calling upon respondent No. 1 to show cause why the impugned order passed ex-parte on 2-2-89, in complaint case No. 53/88, by which the dismissal order dated 15-11-88 of respondent No. 2 was set aside and re-instated with all back wages, purporting to be acting under section 25 (b) of the Employment of Labour (Standing Orders) Act 1965 as well as the order dated 21-6-89 disallowing the Misc. Case No. 2/89 under Order 9(13) Code of Civil Procedure shall not be declared to have been made without any lawful authority and hence is of no legal effect. 

 (D) An order in the form of a writ of certiorari be issued calling upon and directing the respondent No. 1 for hearing the complaint case No. 53/88 de novo as filed by the respondent No. 2 after setting aside the ex parte order date 2-2-89. 

 11. In the cause title of the writ petition the order under challenge is the ex-parte order dated 2-2-89 passed in Complaint Case No. 53 of 1988 but in prayer ''A'' along with the prayer for setting aside the ex-parte order dated 2-2-89 there is a further prayer for setting aside the order dated 21-6-89 passed in Miscellaneous Case No. 1989 disallowing the petitioners'' application for restoration (under Order 9 r.13 of the Code of Civil Procedure) of complaint case No. 53 of 1988. Furthermore, in prayer ''D'' the petitioners demanded a de novo trial of complaint case No. 53 of 1988. But strangely enough the petitioners preferred not to challenge the legality and propriety of the order dated 21-6-89 passed in Miscellaneous Case No. 2 of 1989 in the higher forum. Having chosen not to challenge the order dated 21-6-89 by this writ petition, and the order impugned in this writ petition being a single order i.e. order dated 2-2-89 passed in complaint case No. 53 of 1988 the petitioner''s prayer to that effect is misconceived. Equally misconceived is the prayer for de-novo trial of complaint case No. 53 of 1988. De-novo trial is an alien concept in Labour Law. There is however a provision for de-novo trial in criminal law under section 229 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. Although the second party petitioners challenged the ex parte order dated 2-2-89 passed by the Labour Court by filing Miscellaneous Case No. 2 of 1989 under Order 9 rule 13 of the CPC and the same was rejected by order dated 21-6-89 on contest they preferred no writ petition against that order. Instead they challenged the ex-parte order dated 2-2-89 on the ground that no notice of complaint case No. 53 of 1988 was served upon them. Thus in spite of the argument of Mr Huda that the first party (respondent No. 2 not being a worker, the Labour Court had no jurisdiction to entertain the complaint case filed under section 25 of the Standing Orders Act we will keep our discussion confined within the narrow and limited compass of the ex-parte order dated 2-2-89 because that is the order under challenge in this Writ petition. The jurisdiction of the Labour Court was never challenged, rather in this writ petition in prayer ''D'' the petitioners asked for a fresh or de-novo trial of complaint case No. 53 of 1988 by setting aside the ex-parte order dated 2-2-89. Furthermore, the determination of the question as to whether the first party was or was not a worker is a mixed question both of facts and law and the same being a disputed question of fact this court will not embark on any discussion in that regard. We are called upon to decide whether the Labour Court was justified in passing the ex-parte order dated 2-2-89. The Labour Court held that though the second party was directed to file written statement on 15-1-89 by order dated 26-12-88, on the date fixed the 2nd party remained absent and filed no written statement. The first party was however present by filing hazira. Accordingly, 2-2-89 was fixed for ex-parte disposal of complaint case No. 53 of 1988 on 2-2-89. The first party was present while the second party again remained absent without taking any step. The Labour Court examined the first party as PW 1, perused the papers and documents submitted in support of his case (Exhibits 1-7) and allowed the case directing the second party to reinstate the first party in service with all back wages. In the impugned ex-parte order the Labour Court observed that notices upon the 2nd party petitioners were sent by post. On a reference to the order sheet dated 2-2-89 as contained in Annexure ''C'' it is seen that notices upon the 2nd parties were sent by post (page 12 of the lower court record). The assertions of the first party (respondent No. 2) that in the departmental proceedings against him none of the witnesses were examined in his presence nor was he allowed to cross examine those witnesses and the management on the basis of whimsical report of the Enquiry Committee illegally dismissed him (1st party) from service stood uncontroverted and unrequited. 

 12. From the above discussion and for the foregoing reasons we do not find the Labour Court to have committed any illegality in passing the ex-parte order dated 2-2-89 in complaint case No. 53 of 1988.
